prompt: In user acceptance testing, who decides whether the release is acceptable?
hint: The question changed, and so did the person answering it.

choices.text: The client and the people who will use it
choices.why: Right: the people who will own the product judge whether they can work with it.

choices.text: The test team, comparing results with the requirements
choices.why: That is system testing: the testers judge against the spec.

choices.text: The developer who wrote the release
choices.why: The developer fixes what the client rejects; the verdict is not theirs.

choices.text: An outside auditor hired for the purpose
choices.why: Contractual acceptance may involve one, and UAT is still the client's call.

prompt: Which finding about boxoffice is operational acceptance testing most likely to produce?
hint: Think of the people who run the system, not the people who buy tickets.

choices.text: A student booking is charged 10% off instead of half price
choices.why: A wrong price is functional, and a user would find it.

choices.text: The table of shows scrolls sideways on a phone
choices.why: That is compatibility, found in lesson 7.

choices.text: A restart of the server empties every order
choices.why: Right: whether the system survives being run, restarted and restored is what OAT asks.

choices.text: The tickets field has no label
choices.why: That is accessibility, which lesson 14 covers.

prompt: Match each kind of acceptance testing to what it is.
hint: One description is a system test wearing a client's name.

pairs.right: Staff outside the development team try it in the developers' environment
Some real users try it in their own environment before the general release
The client does real tasks with it and decides
Whoever runs it checks they can back it up, restore it and restart it

right_distractors: The testers rerun their system cases with the client watching

prompt: Rui wants the manager's session on Monday. The regression run on 1.1 ends on Wednesday. What is the best reason to wait?
hint: What is the manager's afternoon worth, and what would it be spent on?

choices.text: UAT is only allowed on a build with no known defects at all
choices.why: Sign-off accepts known defects all the time; what matters is that they are known.

choices.text: The acceptance criteria are written from the regression results
choices.why: Criteria are agreed before the build, not derived from test results.

choices.text: A client must never see a build that has a failing test
choices.why: She will meet the student defect anyway; hiding failures is not the reason.

choices.text: Her one afternoon would go on defects the team could find alone
choices.why: Right: UAT starts when system testing has finished, so the client spends time on what only they know.

prompt: Which of these is a Then that anybody can check on the day?
hint: Could two people disagree about whether it passed?

choices.text: Then students get a fair price
choices.why: Fair to whom? Nobody can fail it, so nobody can pass it.

choices.text: Then the total is R$ 80,00
choices.why: Right: it is on the order page or it is not.

choices.text: Then the right discount is applied to the order
choices.why: Which discount is right is the arithmetic the criterion left out.

choices.text: Then the booking page behaves as the customer expects
choices.why: Expects what? It postpones the argument to sign-off day.

prompt: Put the lines of this scenario in the order they are written.
hint: Situation, action, outcome.
items: Given a confirmed member is booking 5 tickets for Hamlet
trap: The And belongs to the clause it extends.

prompt: In a criterion, the starting situation goes after the keyword ___.
hint: The first of the three.

prompt: A confirmed member, not a student, books 3 tickets for Hamlet at R$ 80,00 each. What total, in reais, should the Then of the criterion state?
hint: Which discounts apply to three tickets, and which is the largest?

prompt: A criterion reads: Given a student who is also a member, booking 5 tickets for The Little Prince, When she books, Then the total is R$ 75,00. It fails. What is wrong with how it was written?
hint: The total itself is right: five at R$ 30,00, half price.

choices.text: R$ 75,00 is not the total R5 gives for that order
choices.why: Five tickets at R$ 30,00 is R$ 150,00, and half is R$ 75,00: the largest discount, 50%.

choices.text: Three discounts are in play at once, so a failure points at none
choices.why: Right: each scenario should check one thing, with everything else held still.

choices.text: A Then must describe a feeling, never a number
choices.why: The reverse: a number is what makes a Then checkable.

choices.text: Only the tester may write a criterion
choices.why: The client writes them, with the tester asking questions.

prompt: During the session the manager stops on the booking page for twenty seconds, looking for something. What does Ana do?
hint: A hesitation is data.

choices.text: Writes down where she stopped and what she seemed to be looking for
choices.why: Right: she was told something no system test measured.

choices.text: Points at the student box, to save time
choices.why: Helping hides exactly what the session exists to find.

choices.text: Takes the mouse and finishes the task for her
choices.why: The client drives; a task the tester finishes tests the tester.

choices.text: Explains that R5 describes where the field is
choices.why: Defending the product with the spec misses what she is showing you.

prompt: Match each thing the manager said to the kind of finding it is.
hint: Three kinds came out of the afternoon.

pairs.left: "No. Students pay half; that's forty reais each."
pairs.right: A defect the team already reported

pairs.left: "At the counter we sell until the curtain goes up."
"Will seven shows make the phone table worse?"

right_distractors: A reason to stop the session

prompt: Why does the counter closing an hour before the show go in as a change request and not a defect report?
hint: Compare the program with R4.

choices.text: The program does what R4 says; R4 is what needs to change
choices.why: Right: the requirement is wrong for the theatre, so the fix starts with the requirement.

choices.text: The manager found it, and only testers file defect reports
choices.why: Anyone can find a defect; what decides is whether the program breaks a requirement.

choices.text: It cannot be shown without waiting until 19:00 on a show day
choices.why: Hard to show is not the same as not a defect.

choices.text: Closing early affects online customers and nobody else
choices.why: It closes the counter too, which is why she objected.

prompt: At the end of the session Ana reads her notes back and the manager confirms each one. What does that step protect against?
hint: Think about the week after the session.

choices.text: Spelling mistakes reaching the defect reports
choices.why: Spelling is the least of it; the content is what gets disputed.

choices.text: The manager dropping findings she would rather not report
choices.why: The notes are a record; nobody edits findings out of them.

choices.text: A finding being disputed later by the person who made it
choices.why: Right: what the client confirmed today is hard to deny next week.

choices.text: A legal requirement that every session has a witness
choices.why: No such rule is involved; it is about agreement, not law.

prompt: Which of these belong in a sign-off for boxoffice 1.1? Choose all that apply.
hint: What would the manager need to point at in six months?

choices.text: The exact build: boxoffice 1.1
choices.why: Yes: "the new version" is not something anyone can check later.

choices.text: Each open defect with the client's decision on it
choices.why: Yes: accepted or must be fixed, in writing.

choices.text: Who accepts, and when
choices.why: Yes: a signature without a name and a date is nobody's.

choices.text: The tester's vote, which settles a tie
choices.why: There is no vote; the decision is the client's.

choices.text: The lines of code that changed in the release
choices.why: That belongs to the release, not to the client's acceptance.

prompt: The manager signs 1.1 provided the student box is removed until it is fixed. What kind of decision is that?
hint: She signed, and something else was written beside the signature.

choices.text: A rejection, since a criterion failed
choices.why: A rejection means no signature; she signed.

choices.text: A plain acceptance of 1.1 as it stands
choices.why: As it stands, the box is still there; she asked for it to go.

choices.text: A conditional acceptance
choices.why: Right: a real decision, whose condition is a promise somebody has to keep.

choices.text: A change request for the next release
choices.why: A change request is a new requirement; this is a condition on accepting this one.

prompt: The manager rejected 1.1. Put what happens next in order.
hint: The fix is checked by the team before it goes back to her.
items: Rui fixes discount, and the build becomes 1.2
A sanity test checks the fix itself
The manager reruns the failed criterion and its neighbours
trap: Regression comes after the fix itself is confirmed.

prompt: Version 1.2 was signed off with the misspelt messages listed as open and accepted. A customer reports them a week later. What does that say about the sign-off?
hint: Read what was written above her name.

choices.text: It was invalid, because a release with open defects cannot be accepted
choices.why: Accepting known defects is what a sign-off often does.

choices.text: The UAT missed them and has to be run again in full
choices.why: They were not missed: they were listed.

choices.text: Ana should not have let a release with open defects be signed by anybody
choices.why: Whether to sign is never the tester's to decide.

choices.text: Nothing went wrong: the client accepted those defects knowingly
choices.why: Right: a sign-off says which defects the client knows of and accepts.

prompt: In the sign-off meeting the manager turns to Ana: "Would you release it?" What answer fits the role this lesson gives her?
hint: An opinion is allowed; a decision is not hers.

choices.text: None: a tester must have no opinion about a release
choices.why: An honest opinion with facts is fine; it just does not decide.

choices.text: Yes, since three of the four criteria passed
choices.why: Counting passes ignores which one failed and what it costs.

choices.text: A decision of her own, since she knows the defects better than anyone
choices.why: Knowing the defects best makes her the best witness, not the judge.

choices.text: Her honest view and its reasons, leaving the choice to the manager
choices.why: Right: she makes the decision informed and leaves it where it belongs.

prompt: The manager writes "students get a fair price". Which question from Ana does most to turn it into a criterion?
hint: A criterion needs a Then that can be seen.

choices.text: What total should a student see for two tickets to Hamlet?
choices.why: Right: the answer is a number on the order page.

choices.text: Is our price fair when compared with what other theatres in São Paulo charge?
choices.why: That reopens the policy, and still gives nothing to check on the screen.

choices.text: Should this be checked in UAT or in system testing?
choices.why: Where it is checked matters less than what counts as passing.

choices.text: Can Rui explain how discount works?
choices.why: The code is not the client's concern; the outcome is.

prompt: Match each person to what they do in boxoffice's acceptance.
hint: One description belongs to nobody in this lesson.

pairs.right: Prepares the session and records what happens

right_distractors: Signs on the client's behalf when the client is busy
